title: Alhamdulillah, thirty-three
hook: all praise to Allah, for what is given

segments.voice: Yesterday: tasbih, subhanallah, glory be to Allah, far above any flaw. Your line was glory. Did something stop you, and did you say the one word? Day one hundred fifteen.

Day three, a long way back now, opened a word that comes out like a reflex. A meal finished: alhamdulillah. A sneeze: alhamdulillah. A friend asked how she's doing: alhamdulillah. The car starting on a cold morning: alhamdulillah. Back then it was a reflex, a word said once and gone. Today it comes back as a count. Thirty-three times, after the prayer, right after the glory. Saying it once without thinking is one thing. Sitting down to say it thirty-three times is another: the list has to keep finding things. Today: the praise.
screen: `BACK ON DAY THREE.` → `A REFLEX, THEN A COUNT.` → `THE LIST HAS TO KEEP FINDING THINGS.`

segments.voice: Alhamdulillah means all praise is for Allah, and saying it is called tahmid. Day three opened the root, h-m-d, and the line Arabic draws between praise and thanks. Today is about two other things: where the word sits, and what the tradition says it weighs. Start with where it sits. It's the opening line of the Fatiha, right after the bismillah: praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds. The Fatiha is recited in every rak'ah of every prayer, so by the time anyone reaches the count afterward, they've already said it more than once. Then the weight. A hadith in Sahih Muslim, from Abu Malik al-Ash'ari, says: alhamdulillah fills the scale. And subhanallah and alhamdulillah, together, fill what's between the heavens and the earth. In the tradition's picture of judgment, deeds are weighed, and this one word fills the pan. Then the smallest version. Another hadith in Muslim says Allah is pleased with the servant who eats a meal and praises Him for it, or drinks a drink and praises Him for it. No great deed. A plate, a cup, and the word. Put those two side by side and the picture is a little strange: the word that fills the scale is the same word said over a glass of water. The thirty-three after the prayer sits between them. Some people use the count as a list, one thing for each joint of the fingers. The obvious things come first. Then the smaller ones: hot water this morning, a door someone held, a knee that didn't ache today.
screen: `ALHAMDULILLAH — ALL PRAISE IS ALLAH'S.` · `IN EVERY RAK'AH, IN THE FATIHA.` · `IT FILLS THE SCALE.` · `A MEAL, A DRINK, AND THE WORD.` · then, large: `ONE THING FOR EACH COUNT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thirty-three on your fingers, with a thing for each. Rest your right hand, palm up. On each joint, name one thing, silently: a person, a meal, a bed, a body that works, a morning. If you pray, say alhamdulillah after each one. If not, say thanks, or just name it. If the things get smaller as you go, let them. Keep going to thirty-three. The bell holds the time.
Tahmid. Saying alhamdulillah, all praise is for Allah, the word that fills the scale; thirty-three after the prayer. Today's word.
Your line: thanks, again. At your next meal and your next drink, say it before the first bite and after the last sip. Day one hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: After each prayer, many Muslims say alhamdulillah thirty-three times following thirty-three subhanallah, and through the day they say it after eating, drinking, sneezing, and when asked how they are.

match.prompt: what's inside the praise — tap the pairs.
pairs: praising Him for them pleases Allah

myth: alhamdulillah and subhanallah together fill what's between heaven and earth
and alhamdulillah alone fills the scale (Muslim, from Abu Malik al-Ash'ari).
the Fatiha begins with the same words
praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds, right after the bismillah.
a hadith says praise only counts for big blessings
Allah is pleased with the one who eats a meal or drinks a drink and praises Him for it (Muslim).

fork.setup: you've just finished a glass of water. according to a hadith in Sahih Muslim, what pleases Allah in that moment?
options: nothing; a drink is too small to count
fork.reveal: Allah is pleased with the servant who eats a meal and praises Him for it, or drinks a drink and praises Him for it (Muslim).

original.note: Arabic: all praise is for Allah. tahmid (تَحْمِيد) is saying it.

trapdoor: what you thought: alhamdulillah means thank God.
what it means: all praise is for Allah: in every rak'ah, thirty-three times after the prayer, and over a single drink.
what a scholar hears: Muslim 223, where alhamdulillah fills the scale and, with subhanallah, what's between heaven and earth; Muslim 2734 on the meal and the drink.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 223 (alhamdulillah fills the scale; with subhanallah, fills what is between the heavens and the earth)
Sahih Muslim 2734 (praising Him for a meal and a drink)
Qur'an 1:2 (praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds)

notes: Hadith numbers cited from memory; please confirm.

In Muslim 223 the wording is that subhanallah and alhamdulillah together fill (or each fills) what is between the heavens and the earth; the script now says 'together'. Please check against the Arabic.
Day 3 of the path taught alhamdulillah as 'thank-you as a reflex'; this day deliberately returns to it.

Editor 2026-10-01: the teach said subhanallah alone fills what is between heaven and earth; Muslim 223 gives that to subhanallah and alhamdulillah together (fixed). 'Every rak'ah begins with it' corrected to 'recited in every rak'ah'. Day 3 already taught the h-m-d root, Muhammad/Ahmad/Hamid, hamd versus shukr and the believer's-affair hadith (Muslim 2999), so those were cut here and the fork and a myth rebuilt on the meal-and-drink hadith; hook no longer assumes the listener says alhamdulillah; practice no longer predicts what the listener will feel; empty closing uplift cut.
